article_title: Rubrics for Examining Historical Thinking Skills in High School World History Activities and Student Work
citation: Hardy, A., Iwatani, E., Means, B., & Seylar, J. (2023). Rubrics for examining historical thinking skills in high school world history activities and student work. Digital Promise. (Original work published 2021). https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/111
title: Use the historical thinking rubrics as a professional learning guide for teachers to analyze their own activities and student work
description: The report recommends that teachers bring in their own activities and a few examples of student work and use the rubrics as a guide to discuss what they observe and possible next steps for students and/or the activity. This positions the rubrics as a shared analytic lens for professional learning communities rather than as a grading tool, supporting reflection on whether assignments open opportunities for historical thinking.
requirements: Teachers supply their own activities and student work samples as discussion artifacts.
constraints: A low score is not intended to imply a student should receive a low grade or that an activity is a poor assignment.
target_learners: high school world history teachers
target_learning_goals: designing activities that provide opportunities for historical thinking
examples: The report's recommended use: teachers score and discuss their own lessons and student work with colleagues using the rubric dimensions.
key_sources: Hardy, A., Iwatani, E., Means, B., & Seylar, J. (2023). Rubrics for examining historical thinking skills in high school world history activities and student work. Digital Promise. (Original work published 2021). https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/111

article_title: Paradise Unified School District: "Building School Mental Health Systems to Support Healing and Recovery through Project Cal-Well"
citation: Paradise Unified School District: Building School Mental Health Systems to Support Healing and Recovery Through Project Cal-Well. (2024). WestEd. https://wested.org
title: RULER social–emotional learning approach adopted districtwide in PUSD
description: RULER is an SEL approach PUSD implemented as a primary objective to enhance student achievement. The name is "an acronym for Recognizing, Understanding, Labeling, Expressing, and Regulating," and it "focuses on developing these five key social–emotional intelligence skills." The district's initiative aims to establish a shared social–emotional vocabulary throughout all grades and schools within the district, positioning SEL as a Tier 1 universal support under Project Cal-Well.
requirements: implementation across all grades and schools to build a shared social–emotional vocabulary
target_learners: all K-12 students across PUSD schools
target_learning_goals: social–emotional intelligence skills: recognizing, understanding, labeling, expressing, and regulating emotions
examples: PUSD adopted RULER districtwide as part of Component 1 universal supports
key_sources: Paradise Unified School District: Building School Mental Health Systems to Support Healing and Recovery Through Project Cal-Well. (2024). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655970

article_title: Local Partnerships, National Impact: Year 1 of the Youth Mental Health Corps
citation: WestEd. (2025). Local Partnerships, National Impact: Year 1 of the Youth Mental Health Corps. https://www.wested.org/resource/building-a-model-of-student-centered-support-through-the-youth-mental-health-corps/
title: Rural multisite rotation: each member works across a rotation of sites to maximize coverage where resources are scarce
description: In rural settings with severe workforce shortages, YMHC members are assigned across a rotation of sites (school, high school, alternative school, public library, restorative justice program) rather than a single placement. The report states this "multisite model, in which each member works across a rotation of sites, addresses the scarcity of resources in rural settings by maximizing one member's impact across diverse settings," keeping members present where students naturally congregate.
requirements: Flexible scheduling based on student needs and site demand
Evening and weekend programming to accommodate rural transportation barriers
constraints: Designed for rural contexts with limited access to mental health services; the report describes it as addressing resource scarcity in such settings
target_learners: rural middle and high school students
target_learning_goals: access to mental health and academic support
connection to school and community resources
examples: Cloquet Public Schools: one member provided more than 620 hours of one-on-one and small group support, with more than 24 students receiving formal support
key_sources: WestEd. (2025). Local Partnerships, National Impact: Year 1 of the Youth Mental Health Corps. https://www.wested.org/resource/building-a-model-of-student-centered-support-through-the-youth-mental-health-corps/

article_title: AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice
citation: Marcos Abreu, Cecilia Stari, Arturo C. Martí. (2026). AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22417
title: Rubric-item guidance table for delegating AI feedback by criterion
description: Table 1 of the article provides per-criterion recommendations for instructors using AI feedback on laboratory reports, elaborated by the authors from the analyzed experience. Objectives may be accepted after general review as the safest item to delegate; theoretical framework feedback, especially formulas and mathematical notation, should be manually reviewed; comments on experimental setup referring to images or apparatus diagrams should be verified before acceptance; data analysis requires prioritized teacher review of calculations, units, graphs, and uncertainties; conclusions should be compared with the graphical evidence cited before validating the score; and the overall assessment should be used only as an orienting input.
requirements: Instructors review AI feedback differentially by rubric item, with heavier verification for items depending on mathematical and visual evidence.
constraints: The table is based on the authors' own elaboration from one analyzed experience in experimental physics laboratory report assessment.
target_learners: higher education instructors assessing physics laboratory reports
target_learning_goals: calibrated use of AI feedback across rubric criteria
examples: The table marks Objectives as "the safest item to delegate to AI" and the Overall assessment as usable "only as an orienting input."
key_sources: Marcos Abreu, Cecilia Stari, Arturo C. Martí. (2026). AI-Assisted Assessment of Experimental Physics Laboratory Reports: Potential, Limitations, and Support for Teaching Practice. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22417

article_title: AlgoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Theoretical Computer Science Education -- A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Algorithm Analysis and Complexity Theory
citation: Sushan Adhikari. (2026). AlgoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Theoretical Computer Science Education — A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Algorithm Analysis and Complexity Theory. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14572
title: Rubric-based pedagogical quality scoring as a primary evaluation metric for educational AI in formal domains
description: The article defines a composite pedagogical quality score on [0,1] as the mean of six binary criteria applied per response: step-by-step exposition, correct mathematical notation, worked example, query coverage, explanation depth, and proof-step granularity. Because "equivalent mathematical proofs can use substantially different wording", the authors argue this rubric "captures educational value independently of surface wording" and is a more appropriate primary metric than ROUGE or BLEU for mathematical educational AI, offering a reusable benchmark methodology.
requirements: Reference answers or rubric application by domain instructors; consistent application across all responses
constraints: Educational effectiveness is inferred from the rubric rather than measured learning outcomes; no controlled user study was conducted
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in formal domains such as theoretical computer science
target_learning_goals: evaluating the instructional quality of AI-generated explanations of mathematical proofs
examples: Applied consistently to all 179 AlgoRAG responses, yielding 0.7620 overall and a 0.6629–0.8250 range across topics
key_sources: Sushan Adhikari. (2026). AlgoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Theoretical Computer Science Education — A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Algorithm Analysis and Complexity Theory. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14572

article_title: Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human-Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation
citation: Pei-Yu Tseng, Mahir Akgun, and Peng Liu. (2026). Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human–Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23629
title: Rubric revision pattern: separate construct from surface cues, specify valid evidence, make scoring logic operational, and make adjacent boundaries explicit
description: When machine raters misread rubric constructs, the article distills four revision principles from its mismatch analysis. For openness: (P1) separate the intended construct from misleading surface cues, making clear that openness depends on response-space breadth rather than on whether a question appears to have a single correct answer, and (P2) specify what counts as valid evidence for each score level. For depth: (P3) make the scoring logic operational rather than purely descriptive, with a classification structure, examples, and an explicit decision rule, and (P4) make adjacent score boundaries explicit.
requirements: Requires diagnosing recurring machine scoring heuristics that diverge from the rubric's intended meaning before revising
constraints: Derived from mismatches observed for the openness and depth dimensions in one LLM-based evaluation workflow; relevance and clarity already aligned near-perfectly
target_learners: undergraduate Cybersecurity students in an intermediate-level statistics course
target_learning_goals: accurate machine evaluation of pretest question openness and cognitive depth
examples: The machine treated explanatory wording such as explain or why as evidence of analytical reasoning and treated procedural articulation as evaluative synthesis; the revised rubric addressed these with explicit decision rules
key_sources: Pei-Yu Tseng, Mahir Akgun, and Peng Liu. (2026). Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human–Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23629

article_title: An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria
citation: Nwogo, E. U., Ihianle, I. K., Machado, P., Bird, J. J., Lotfi, A., Shuaib, A. A., Akinwumi, I. I., & Oluranti, J. (2026). An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15738
title: Use a transparent rule-based performance-scoring formula combining academic scores with non-cognitive attributes to keep adaptive educational decisions interpretable and accountable
description: The platform computes a final performance score from the academic score A and averaged non-cognitive scores (age, health status, motivation, study time, language proficiency, prior experience) using an explicit formula with a maximum non-cognitive weight of 0.1. The authors state that "by explicitly defining the contribution of each factor, the system avoids the opacity often associated with purely data-driven models, making it suitable for educational environments where accountability is essential". The score then drives personalised content delivery and targeted feedback interventions.
requirements: Explicit definition of each factor's contribution; selected non-cognitive attributes must be collected and maintained in learner profiles
constraints: The article states machine learning-based approaches could be applied, but a rule-based method was adopted for clarity, interpretability, and suitability for educational decision-making; the non-cognitive weight is capped at 0.1
target_learners: Learners in under-resourced educational systems where accountability and transparency in assessment are required
target_learning_goals: Holistic learner assessment beyond academic achievement and adaptive personalised feedback
examples: Two student cases computed with Equation (3): Student 1 (academic 83.75, performance 86.15) received a concise explanation, Student 2 (academic 40.00, performance 42.30) received a more scaffolded one
key_sources: Nwogo, E. U., Ihianle, I. K., Machado, P., Bird, J. J., Lotfi, A., Shuaib, A. A., Akinwumi, I. I., & Oluranti, J. (2026). An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15738

article_title: REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading
citation: Chengshuai Zhao, Fan Zhang, Kumar Satvik Chaudhary, Yiwen Li, Lo Pang-Yun Ting, Ying-Chih Chen, Huan Liu. (2025). REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading. https://github.com/scott-f-zhang/REC-CBM
title: Route automated grading predictions through human-interpretable rubric-level concepts so educators can inspect, verify, and intervene
description: In high-stakes educational assessment, raw accuracy alone is insufficient; instructors need to understand why a score was produced and how to intervene on questionable judgments. Routing grading predictions through human-interpretable rubric-level concepts provides a mechanistic guarantee of transparency, decomposing the final grade into rubric-level concept predictions that educators can examine or modify. The article states this enables educators to "inspect, verify, and intervene on reasoning," supporting intervention and auditing and promoting pedagogical usefulness through concept-level outputs aligned with feedback categories.
requirements: Rubric-aligned concept annotations must cover the dominant rubric axes that determine the holistic grade, be non-redundant, and have ordinally interpretable anchored descriptors
constraints: Standard CBMs assume shared latent space and evenly spaced categories, requiring rubric-aware encoding and ordinal calibration to work well for fine-grained grading
target_learners: educators and instructors using automated grading systems
target_learning_goals: trustworthy and transparent automated grading of open-ended student responses
examples: REC-CBM implements this by decomposing grading into per-concept ordinal predictions with token-level attention evidence, corrected posteriors, and additive per-concept contributions to the grade logit
key_sources: Chengshuai Zhao, Fan Zhang, Kumar Satvik Chaudhary, Yiwen Li, Lo Pang-Yun Ting, Ying-Chih Chen, Huan Liu. (2025). REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading. https://github.com/scott-f-zhang/REC-CBM

article_title: DIFFERENTIAL EFFECTS OF PROMPTS AND RECASTS IN FORM-FOCUSED INSTRUCTION
citation: Roy Lyster. (2004). DIFFERENTIAL EFFECTS OF PROMPTS AND RECASTS IN FORM-FOCUSED INSTRUCTION. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 26, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263104263021
title: Rule-based representation and proceduralization account of form-focused instruction effects
description: The article interprets its findings through a skill-acquisition account in which form-focused instruction helps L2 learners build explicit, rule-based representations of grammatical forms and then proceduralize that knowledge through practice and feedback. Prompts are positioned as especially suited to this account because they push learners to produce and self-repair target forms, supporting the move from declarative rule knowledge toward proceduralized use, whereas recasts provide only models of the correct form.
requirements: Explicit attention to the target form (e.g., noun endings predicting gender)
Opportunities for practice associating forms with their targets
constraints: Framed here as a means of enabling acquisition of grammatical gender representations specifically; the account is the authors' interpretation of the task results
target_learners: L2 learners in immersion classrooms
target_learning_goals: Acquiring rule-based representations of grammatical gender and proceduralizing knowledge of emerging forms
key_sources: Roy Lyster. (2004). DIFFERENTIAL EFFECTS OF PROMPTS AND RECASTS IN FORM-FOCUSED INSTRUCTION. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 26, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263104263021

article_title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
citation: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3
title: Rubrics should be co-created and used dialogically with exemplars, not as checklists that supplant judgement
description: The paper argues rubrics act as a scaffold for evaluative judgement only when designed and used to reflect the nuanced understandings of quality experts use. Recommended improvements include formative use, co-creation with students to build shared understanding of criteria, dialogic discussion of descriptors, use alongside exemplars, and movement "back and forth from work to rubrics then to the work to formulate deeper understandings of quality".
requirements: Students must be involved in discussing criteria; rubrics must represent how evaluative judgements are actually made in the discipline
constraints: Rubrics as present/absent checklists, standardised templates, or rubrics that supplant evaluative judgement are identified as sub-optimal; applying a rubric does not imply judgement without one
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding and applying quality criteria
examples: The paper cites Fraile et al. (2016) on student co-creation of rubrics involving collective brainstorming of criteria with teacher support
key_sources: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3

article_title: Rules Versus Drill in Teaching Spelling.
citation: Turner, E. A.; Markus, H. P. (1912). Rules versus drill in teaching spelling; Some results in manual training. Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Pair spelling-rule instruction with type words and minimal drill when transfer to new words is the goal
description: This principle holds that spelling instruction which teaches rules and associates them with type words, requiring only a minimum of drill, is the arrangement to use when the instructional goal includes transfer to new, similar words. In the reported experiment, the rules group's instruction consisted of "three 25-minute exercises, in two of which rules were taught and associated with type words and a minimum of drill required." The rules group showed a distinct advantage on the new-word transfer test, supporting the principle for that outcome.
requirements: Instruction must include explicit teaching of rules associated with type words, not rules alone; the article's condition paired rules with type words across two of three 25-minute exercises.
constraints: The article's evidence comes from one small parallel-group experiment (16 pupils per group) with eighth-grade pupils, separate teachers per group, and no time on the words outside the 25-minute exercises; the drill group retained repeated words relatively better after five days.
target_learners: eighth-grade pupils
target_learning_goals: spelling of new words similar to taught words
examples: Group II received three 25-minute exercises in which rules were taught and associated with type words with a minimum of drill, and outperformed the drill-only group on the new-word 'D' test.
key_sources: Turner, E. A.; Markus, H. P. (1912). Rules versus drill in teaching spelling; Some results in manual training. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0069736

article_title: The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages
citation: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y
title: Russell's core affect model maps the four instructor emotions onto positive–negative and active–passive dimensions
description: The article adapts Russell's model of core affect as the taxonomy underlying its four instructor emotions. As printed, "Russell's (1980, 2003) model of core affect represents human emotion along two orthogonal dimensions: a positive–negative dimension and an active–passive dimension." The animated instructor was designed to convey the emotion of each of the four quadrants, "which we have labeled as happy (positive/active), content (positive/passive), frustrated (negative/active), and bored (negative/passive)", a classification the authors note is similar to Pekrun and Perry's taxonomy of achievement emotions. The positivity hypothesis tested in the study focuses on the positive–negative dimension of this space.
requirements: Classifying an instructor's emotional display requires locating it on both the positive–negative and the active–passive dimensions
constraints: The study's predictions focus on the positive–negative dimension rather than the full two-dimensional space
target_learners: adult online learners in multimedia instructional settings
target_learning_goals: recognizing instructor emotional tone along valence and activity dimensions
key_sources: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y

article_title: Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing
citation: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2
title: Rubric-point-decomposed automated feedback for iterative proof revision
description: A lesson-level pattern in which a submitted proof is decomposed by rubric points and the student receives targeted feedback identifying which specific step of the proof is problematic, then revises and resubmits. The rubric was designed so that each point addresses a known misconception about induction proofs, allowing errors to be localized rather than reported as a single holistic score.
requirements: A rubric whose points align with documented misconceptions in the target proof technique, and a grading model accurate enough per point to avoid misleading feedback
constraints: Feedback identifies the failing rubric point but does not explain how to fix the error, which some students found insufficiently elaborated
target_learners: Undergraduate students learning proof by induction
target_learning_goals: Producing a complete and logically correct induction proof
examples: Students in the study submitted proofs and received rubric-point-level feedback indicating which parts of their proof were incorrect, then revised their proofs
key_sources: Zhao, C., Silva, M., & Poulsen, S. (2025). Autograding Mathematical Induction Proofs with Natural Language Processing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3202–3232. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00498-2

article_title: Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics
citation: Khachatryan, G. A., Romashov, A. V., Khachatryan, A. R., Gaudino, S. J., Khachatryan, J. M., Guarian, K. R., & Yufa, N. V. (2014). Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0019-7
title: Russian mathematics instruction principles: a set of shared salient practices extracted from expert teachers
description: Interviews with the expert teacher panel surfaced numerous shared methods, leading the authors to speak of a single "Russian mathematics education tradition". The article enumerates its salient aspects: guided instruction rather than pure discovery; fading from worked examples to independent problem solving; motivating new constructs before formal definitions; organizing knowledge around mathematically meaningful structures (e.g., treating decimals as a special case of fractions); explicit rules and definitions; mathematical precision; explanatory feedback referring back to definitions and rules; automaticity through spaced practice; breaking difficult concepts into constituent components; and an overriding "anti-principle" placing the accumulated content-specific experience of practitioners above any general principles.
requirements: The practices are content-specific and were held together by a community of teachers whose accumulated experience governs pedagogical decisions
constraints: The article contrasts these with United States practices as observed in this project and cited literature, not as a controlled comparison
target_learners: School mathematics students, especially struggling or average students in guided instruction
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding, procedural fluency and automaticity, mathematical precision, and coherent knowledge structures in mathematics
examples: Before defining factors, students solve: among how many children can 18 apples be divided evenly? The meaningful list of divisors then motivates the term
key_sources: Khachatryan, G. A., Romashov, A. V., Khachatryan, A. R., Gaudino, S. J., Khachatryan, J. M., Guarian, K. R., & Yufa, N. V. (2014). Reasoning Mind Genie 2: An Intelligent Tutoring System as a Vehicle for International Transfer of Instructional Methods in Mathematics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0019-7

article_title: Automated Essay Scoring and the Deep Learning Black Box: How Are Rubric Scores Determined?
citation: Kumar, V. S., & Boulanger, D. (2020). Automated Essay Scoring and the Deep Learning Black Box: How Are Rubric Scores Determined? International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00211-5
title: Rubric-level prediction as a route to interpretable, trustable AES with human-in-the-loop assessment
description: The article's organizing account holds that predicting constituent rubric scores (Ideas, Organization, Style, Conventions) rather than only holistic scores "reveals the reasoning behind AIED-based AES systems". Because rubric scales are narrower (0–6 vs 0–24), each rubric score offers more training examples per competence, and feature-importance analysis per rubric model provides high-level explanations of predicted scores. The framework ties interpretability to trustworthiness and to human-in-the-loop verification of machine grading.
requirements: Hand-graded essays with rubric-level labels (as in ASAP D7)
Sufficient samples per rubric score for model training
constraints: The article states it is beyond the scope of the study to verify whether holistic prediction through rubric scores is more accurate, and that less accurate models may be more interpretable
target_learners: Grade 7–10 student writers
target_learning_goals: Writing quality across ideas, organization, style, and conventions
examples: The study trained six MLP architectures on 397 SALAT-derived writing features to predict D7's four rubric scores and used permutation importance to rank features per rubric
key_sources: Kumar, V. S., & Boulanger, D. (2020). Automated Essay Scoring and the Deep Learning Black Box: How Are Rubric Scores Determined? International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00211-5

article_title: The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology
citation: Richard E. West, Peg Ertmer, Susan McKenney. (2020). The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09770-9
title: Five-criterion rubric for evaluating theoretical scholarship: instructive, scholarly, practical, logical, writing quality
description: The guest editors created an evaluative rubric for reviewers of theoretical papers, rating each criterion on a scale of 1 to 3. The five criteria are that "The article should be… INSTRUCTIVE", SCHOLARLY, PRACTICAL, LOGICAL, and of high WRITING QUALITY. Instructive asks whether the theoretical framework expands current perspective and makes a genuine contribution; scholarly asks whether it suggests new research and/or development directions; practical asks whether it suggests new recommendations for Learning, Design, and Technology practice; logical asks whether the article provides a strong, logical argument using existing literature or evidence; and writing quality covers clarity of expression, flow, and effective use of headings and visuals.
requirements: Reviewers rate each paper on a scale of 1 to 3 for each criterion
constraints: The editors state they do not argue this is the perfect set of criteria, but offer it as a useful start
target_learners: journal reviewers and editors in learning design and technology
target_learning_goals: assessing the rigor and quality of theoretical scholarship
examples: The rubric was offered to the reviewers of the special issue and used to select the articles published in it
key_sources: Richard E. West, Peg Ertmer, Susan McKenney. (2020). The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09770-9

article_title: Development and validation of a measure of authentic online work
citation: Darling-Aduana, J. (2021). Development and validation of a measure of authentic online work. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10007-6
title: Use a validated authenticity rubric to support researcher, developer, and school-based continuous improvement of online tasks
description: The article recommends deploying the validated Authentic Online Work Rubric as a measurement tool within improvement processes. It states the rubric "is targeted for use in the evaluation of learning tasks and assessments in online instructional settings to support researcher, developer, and school-based continuous improvement processes." This positions lesson-level authenticity measurement as actionable feedback for multiple stakeholders.
requirements: Observers must be trained on the rubric's rating anchors and lesson coding conventions
The scale should be applied in online instructional settings where it was validated
constraints: The communication and collaboration subscale remains unvalidated, so full-scale use in alternative settings is not yet supported
target_learners: secondary online course students
target_learning_goals: evaluating and improving authenticity of online learning tasks and assessments
examples: Data were collected from online courses developed by one of the largest online course providers in the United States, with lesson-level coefficients generated for both subscales
key_sources: Darling-Aduana, J. (2021). Development and validation of a measure of authentic online work. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10007-6

article_title: Rubric use in dental education: a systematic review of design, implementation, and educational impact.
citation: Gadbail Amol Ramchandra, Gondivkar Shailesh M., Yuwanati Monal B., Sonone Archana, Dhamande Mithilesh, Panchbhai Aarati, Hande Alka H., Patil Swati, Sarode Sachin C. (2026). Rubric use in dental education: a systematic review of design, implementation, and educational impact. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09218-3
title: Rubrics as criterion-referenced evaluation instruments with analytic and holistic types
description: A rubric is defined by the review as "an evaluation instrument that delineates explicit criteria alongside graduated levels of achievement", facilitating criterion-referenced feedback for formative and summative purposes. The review distinguishes rubrics from checklists, which simply mark task completion, and numeric rating scales, which give global scores without criterion-specific feedback. It organizes rubrics into two types: "analytic where individual criteria are assessed separately and holistic assessment where a student's overall performance is assessed via a single comprehensive rubric". This taxonomy frames the review's synthesis of rubric design and implementation in dental education.
requirements: Rubrics require explicit criteria paired with graduated performance levels and descriptive feedback for each level to deliver criterion-referenced feedback
constraints: The review notes limited cross-institutional validation restricts generalizability of rubric effectiveness claims across all dental education contexts
target_learners: undergraduate dental students
postgraduate dental students
target_learning_goals: clinical competency assessment
psychomotor skills
clinical judgment
professional behaviors
self-assessment and reflective practice
examples: Most included studies (20/23) applied analytic rubrics providing criterion-specific scoring across dental specialties including restorative dentistry, periodontics, endodontics, prosthodontics, and oral surgery
key_sources: Gadbail Amol Ramchandra, Gondivkar Shailesh M., Yuwanati Monal B., Sonone Archana, Dhamande Mithilesh, Panchbhai Aarati, Hande Alka H., Patil Swati, Sarode Sachin C. (2026). Rubric use in dental education: a systematic review of design, implementation, and educational impact. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09218-3

article_title: The Effectiveness of Educational Games on Scientific Concepts Acquisition in First Grade Students in Science
citation: Mohammad Hasan Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Effectiveness of Educational Games on Scientific Concepts Acquisition in the First Grade Students in Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.3. https://www.iiste.org
title: Game-based lessons structured as rule-governed sensory activities with defined objectives
description: Each lesson pairs a named educational game with explicit objectives and a scripted procedure in which the teacher presents objects or stimuli, the learner experiences a sensory gap (e.g. eyes closed), and the learner then names or distinguishes the concepts. Games are "purposeful activities first graders have practiced either individually or in groups" under "pre-set rules for achieving particular objectives". The pattern grounds abstract concepts (sight, colors, size, distance) in direct tangible experience.
requirements: Pre-set rules and particular objectives per game
Materials such as cut-outs, balls, shapes and colored objects
constraints: Demonstrated with first graders on sensory-unit content
target_learners: first grade students
target_learning_goals: recognizing shapes, colors, size and distance concepts
acquiring five-senses scientific concepts
examples: The Close your eyes lesson asks students to identify shapes, colors, near/far people and big/small bears before and after opening their eyes
key_sources: Mohammad Hasan Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Effectiveness of Educational Games on Scientific Concepts Acquisition in the First Grade Students in Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1089788

article_title: The Effects of Portfolio Assessment on Writing of EFL Students
citation: Behzad Nezakatgoo. (2011). The Effects of Portfolio Assessment on Writing of EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 4(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n2p231
title: Use a common rubric and trained readers to address inter-rater reliability in portfolio assessment
description: To counter criticisms that portfolio assessment increases subjectivity, the article states that "Portfolio assessment requires that readers be trained to agree and to score papers based on a common rubric that describes numerical points". Rubrics should cover development and organization, fluency of idea description, and mechanics. In the study itself, an independent scorer evaluated final portfolios to address inter-rater reliability.
requirements: Readers trained to agree and score with a common rubric
Rubrics covering development, organization, fluency, and mechanics
constraints: Without sufficiently high inter-rater reliability, scores cannot be considered valid
target_learners: EFL and ESL writing students
target_learning_goals: Reliable and valid assessment of writing portfolios
examples: The study invited an independent scorer to evaluate final assessment of portfolios to eliminate instructor bias
key_sources: Behzad Nezakatgoo. (2011). The Effects of Portfolio Assessment on Writing of EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 4(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n2p231

article_title: Using Rubrics as an Instructional Tool in EFL Writing Courses
citation: Turgut, F., & Kayaoğlu, M. N. (2015). Using rubrics as an instructional tool in EFL writing courses. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 11(1), 47-58. http://www.jlls.org
title: Rubrics as instructional tools: holistic and analytic scoring guides that make assessment criteria visible to learners
description: A rubric is defined in the article as "a descriptive list of the criteria which teachers employ to judge their students’ work". Holistic rubrics score the overall product as a whole, while analytic rubrics score separate parts and sum them, allowing a profile of strengths and weaknesses and specific feedback. Originally assessment-only tools, rubrics are reframed here as teaching tools that support student learning, used in this study via the adapted ESL Composition Profile with content, organization, vocabulary, language use and mechanics components.
requirements: Students need several opportunities of working with real samples of writing to internalize each trait, with the guidance of an expert teacher
constraints: Simply handing students a rubric without guided practice is stated to fail to enable students to develop the thinking skills the rubric's standards require
target_learners: intermediate-level university EFL students in intensive English preparatory programs
target_learning_goals: EFL writing performance across content, organization, vocabulary, language use and mechanics
examples: The study used an adapted ESL Composition Profile (Jacobs et al., 1981) with five components at four performance levels on a 100-point scale, with modified numerical weights
key_sources: Turgut, F., & Kayaoğlu, M. N. (2015). Using rubrics as an instructional tool in EFL writing courses. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 11(1), 47-58. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105202

article_title: Collaborative Learning Supported by Rubrics Improves Critical Thinking
citation: Carlos Saiz, Silvia F. Rivas and Sonia Olivares. (2015). Collaborative learning supported by rubrics improves critical thinking. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotl.v15i1.12905
title: Design critical thinking activities with task-specific rubrics and orient students' own activity rather than solving problems for them
description: The article recommends that active student participation be accompanied by specific instructions: the instructor dedicates more time to directing and orienting students' work and less time to solving the problems posed, and each task or problem gets a specific rubric. The authors state that "The method employing rubrics is one of the most efficient ways of quantifying qualitative tasks and guiding learning in a highly concrete and specific manner", so students know which aspects to work, their relevance, the points they would earn, and the strategies required.
requirements: A specific rubric elaborated for each of the tasks or problems posed
Instructor time reallocated from solving problems to orienting students' work
constraints: The article links the approach to its own program; decision making did not benefit from the change in instruction
target_learners: first-year university students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking competencies such as argumentation
examples: Chart 1 shows the argumentation rubric detailing and scoring comprehension, precision in drafting ideas, structure, and assessment, with a maximum total score of 100
key_sources: Carlos Saiz, Silvia F. Rivas and Sonia Olivares. (2015). Collaborative learning supported by rubrics improves critical thinking. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Vol. 15, No. 1. https://doi.org/10.14434/josotl.v15i1.12905

article_title: Using Propensity Score Weighting to Reduce Selection Bias in Large-Scale Data Sets
citation: Crystal D. Bishop, Walter L. Leite, and Patricia A. Snyder. (2018). Using Propensity Score Weighting to Reduce Selection Bias in Large-Scale Data Sets. Journal of Early Intervention. https://doi.org/10.1177/1053815118793430
title: Rubin's potential outcomes framework for estimating treatment effects with survey data
description: The article presents Rubin's potential outcomes framework as the conceptual basis for estimating treatment effects from survey data. It assumes all individuals have potential outcomes for each treatment condition, only one of which is observed. Two estimands are described: the ATE, "used to examine the effect of a treatment for all individuals," and the ATT, used for individuals who received treatment. Unbiased estimates require strong ignorability of treatment assignment and the overlap assumption.
requirements: Strong ignorability of treatment assignment: selection probabilities conditional on baseline covariates must be uncorrelated with potential outcome distributions
The overlap assumption: probability of treatment assignment is neither zero nor one for any participant
constraints: With nonrandomly assigned survey data, strong ignorability is often not met and selection bias exists
target_learners: young children with or at risk for developmental delays and their families in early intervention research
target_learning_goals: estimating plausible causal effects of malleable factors on child developmental outcomes from longitudinal survey data
examples: The article illustrates ATE with attendance at a voluntary pre-kindergarten program for children at risk for developmental delays, and ATT with preschool special education services for preschool children with disabilities
key_sources: Crystal D. Bishop, Walter L. Leite, and Patricia A. Snyder. (2018). Using Propensity Score Weighting to Reduce Selection Bias in Large-Scale Data Sets. Journal of Early Intervention. https://doi.org/10.1177/1053815118793430

article_title: The Effect of EFL Teachers' Training in Rural West China: Evidence from Phonics-Oriented Program
citation: Kang, Y., & Liang, L. (2018). The Effect of EFL Teachers’ Training in Rural West China: Evidence From Phonics-oriented Program. English Language Teaching, 11(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n3p40
title: In-service professional support system for rural EFL teachers
description: After training, a professional support system was constructed involving an expert group, English teaching specialists, education bureau directors, headmasters, core EFL teachers and ordinary EFL teachers, with core teachers connecting all actors. "A learning community of 5 to10 people was built up in central school districts" carrying out weekly face-to-face teaching-research activities, plus a virtual platform (http://www.mtevideo.cn) with regularly-updated resources and a forum. The system was intended to reduce frustration when teachers met difficulties in teaching practice.
requirements: Core EFL teachers to convene weekly learning-community activities
Access to teaching resources such as workbooks, cards, CDs and course-wares, and an online platform for virtual communication
constraints: The website was closed four years later after fulfilling its responsibilities, and most rural schools have only one English teacher, limiting local oral-English practice opportunities
target_learners: In-service rural primary EFL teachers
target_learning_goals: Sustained professional development in English teaching
Applying phonics in classroom practice
examples: Weekly face-to-face activities included teaching plan designing, classroom observation, comments and feedbacks
key_sources: Kang, Y., & Liang, L. (2018). The Effect of EFL Teachers’ Training in Rural West China: Evidence From Phonics-oriented Program. English Language Teaching, 11(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n3p40

article_title: Preventive Initiatives to Promote Psychological Adjustment among Primary Students: Findings of RULER Approach in Spanish Public Schools
citation: Castillo-Gualda, R., Moraleda, A., & Brackett, M. A. (2023). Preventive Initiatives to Promote Psychological Adjustment Among Primary Students: Findings of RULER Approach in Spanish Public Schools. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 12(2), pp. 206-232. https://doi.org/10.17583/ijep.10970
title: RULER approach: a systemic SEL approach based on emotional intelligence theory with a theory of change starting from adult training
description: RULER (Recognizing, Understanding, Labeling, Expressing, Regulating) is described as "a systemic approach based on emotional intelligence theory" that "provides a series of tools to the entire educational community" to develop five emotion skills. Its "theory of change is primarily based on the training of adults", inclusion of RULER skills in school culture, integration of tools in pedagogy, and subsequent coursework adapted to students' development. The four tools named are the Charter, Mood Meter, Meta-Moment, and Blueprint.
requirements: Teacher professional development (15 hours plus 3 hours follow-up) and implementation guidelines throughout the school year
constraints: The pathway to student development runs through adult intervention; effects in this study appeared only in the 10-12 age group
target_learners: Primary school students ages 6-12
Teachers and the whole educational community
target_learning_goals: Recognizing, understanding, labeling, expressing, and regulating emotions
examples: Teachers received 4 in-person training sessions (15 hours) on RULER abilities and the four tools, followed by a 3-hour implementation and follow-up phase introducing skills and lessons to students
key_sources: Castillo-Gualda, R., Moraleda, A., & Brackett, M. A. (2023). Preventive Initiatives to Promote Psychological Adjustment Among Primary Students: Findings of RULER Approach in Spanish Public Schools. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 12(2), pp. 206-232. https://doi.org/10.17583/ijep.10970

article_title: Dynamic CBME in action: rule-based digital case-based learning to evaluate antibiotic-stewardship reasoning in MBBS learners.
citation: Sunil Kumar D, Sucheta Dandekar, G. Hari Prakash. (2026). Dynamic CBME in action: rule-based digital case-based learning to evaluate antibiotic-stewardship reasoning in MBBS learners. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09810-7
title: Rule-based Digital Case-Based Learning (DCBL) module with algorithm-triggered formative feedback
description: A digital learning module comprising three online micro-cases (URTI, UTI, acute watery diarrhoea) built on "a rule-based branching logic architecture". At each decision node, "pre-authored, expert-reviewed formative feedback" was automatically triggered based on the learner's selection. The platform deliberately used no generative AI or large language model. Cases were designed to activate illness-script formation consistent with script theory.
requirements: Requires pre-authored, expert-reviewed feedback content at each decision node
Requires branching clinical logic with predefined response options
constraints: The platform did not use generative artificial intelligence and did not generate de novo adaptive text
target_learners: Third- and fourth-phase MBBS learners
target_learning_goals: Antibiotic-stewardship clinical reasoning
Clinical decision-making under uncertainty
examples: Three micro-cases with two to three decision nodes each, completed in a single 45-60 minute sitting
key_sources: Sunil Kumar D, Sucheta Dandekar, G. Hari Prakash. (2026). Dynamic CBME in action: rule-based digital case-based learning to evaluate antibiotic-stewardship reasoning in MBBS learners. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09810-7

article_title: Teaching persuasive essay writing online to first-year undergraduates: A phenomenological study of instructional design and learning experiences.
citation: Karim, K. A., Al Mamun, M. A., Sultana, S., & Kabilan, M. K. (2026). Teaching persuasive essay writing online to first-year undergraduates: A phenomenological study of instructional design and learning experiences. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353171
title: Rubric-guided checklist for structured peer feedback on persuasive essays
description: A detailed checklist was used to structure peer feedback across four essay components: outline, introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion. Each component had specific criteria (e.g., "Does the thesis statement clearly express the main claim and the 3 reasons?"). Groups exchanged essays, identified strengths ('did well') before areas for improvement ('could improve'), and delivered feedback verbally during live sessions with the instructor present as moderator.
requirements: Instructor-assigned group pairings for essay exchange
Live sessions for verbal feedback delivery
Teacher moderation of feedback sessions
constraints: Implemented as group-level rather than individual peer review
target_learners: First-year undergraduates in online courses
target_learning_goals: Evaluating persuasive essay quality
Providing constructive peer feedback
key_sources: Karim, K. A., Al Mamun, M. A., Sultana, S., & Kabilan, M. K. (2026). Teaching persuasive essay writing online to first-year undergraduates: A phenomenological study of instructional design and learning experiences. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353171

article_title: Effectiveness of a structured rubric-based assessment in preclinical crown preparation training: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Chen Marie Fung Ying, Mundathaje Mahesh, Natarajan Srikant, Bajantri Prashant, Mukherjee Sandipan. (2026). Effectiveness of a structured rubric-based assessment in preclinical crown preparation training: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08667-y
title: Rubric-based assessment grounded in self-regulated learning and constructive alignment
description: The article frames analytical rubrics within self-regulated learning and constructive alignment: "Self-regulated learning emphasizes learners’ active engagement in goal setting, self-monitoring, and reflection, processes that are facilitated when assessment criteria are explicit and transparent." By aligning objectives, activities, and assessment criteria, rubric-based assessment supports constructive alignment, providing a theoretical basis for how structured assessment influences preclinical performance.
requirements: Assessment criteria must be explicit and transparent for learners to self-monitor and adjust learning strategies
target_learners: undergraduate dental students in preclinical courses
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
psychomotor skill acquisition
key_sources: Chen Marie Fung Ying, Mundathaje Mahesh, Natarajan Srikant, Bajantri Prashant, Mukherjee Sandipan. (2026). article_title: Objective Assessment of Ergonomics and Performance of Thoracic Surgeons During Real-Life Anatomical Robotic Pulmonary Resections.
citation: Elkhouly AG, Santhirakumaran G, Shanahan B, Batchelor T, Wilson H, Waller D, Stamenkovic S, Lau K. (2025). Objective Assessment of Ergonomics and Performance of Thoracic Surgeons During Real-Life Anatomical Robotic Pulmonary Resections. Interdisciplinary Cardiovascular and Thoracic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1093/icvts/ivaf180
title: RULA (rapid upper limb assessment) score as an ergonomic-risk measure for robotic surgeons
description: The rapid upper limb assessment scale is used in this study to estimate ergonomic risk and surgeon posture during robotic procedures. The article describes it as "a validated and dependable tool used to calculate a surgeon's work-related ergonomics during robotic procedures, where lower scores equate to better ergonomics." It primarily evaluates the upper body and suits seated individuals; scores of 1-2 are satisfactory, 3-4 low risk, 5-6 medium risk warranting early investigation and modification, and 7 high risk requiring immediate action. Joint angles measured in Kinovea are converted into the RULA score.
requirements: Measurement of surgeons' joint angles (via video analysis) during the procedure; the tool is suitable for individuals in a seated position
constraints: Assesses primarily the upper body; interpretation bands run from 1-2 (satisfactory) to 7 (high risk requiring immediate action)
target_learners: surgeons performing robot-assisted thoracic surgery
target_learning_goals: assessing and reducing ergonomic risk and work-related musculoskeletal disorder risk during surgical training and practice
examples: Applied to arterial and venous dissection/division in robotic segmentectomy and lobectomy; expert median score 4 (low MSD risk) and novice median 5 (moderate risk), with the neck and elbow the joints most deviating from neutral angles
key_sources: Elkhouly AG, Santhirakumaran G, Shanahan B, Batchelor T, Wilson H, Waller D, Stamenkovic S, Lau K. (2025). Objective Assessment of Ergonomics and Performance of Thoracic Surgeons During Real-Life Anatomical Robotic Pulmonary Resections. Interdisciplinary Cardiovascular and Thoracic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1093/icvts/ivaf180

article_title: The Dynamics of Students' Behaviors and Reasoning during Collaborative Physics Tutorial Sessions
citation: Conlin, L. D., Gupta, A., Scherr, R. E., & Hammer, D. (2006). The Dynamics of Students' Behaviors and Reasoning during Collaborative Physics Tutorial Sessions. Physics Education Research Conference proceedings record. https://www.compadre.org/PER/
title: Russ's framework for recognizing mechanistic reasoning as a hierarchy of elements culminating in chaining
description: The article uses Russ's coding scheme to recognize mechanistic reasoning in students' verbal responses, organized as "a hierarchy of increasing quality of evidence": describing the target phenomenon, set-up conditions, entities, actions, properties of entities, organization of entities, and chaining. Chaining, the most complete element, links several elements together to make predictions or reason about the past, and the framework assesses reasoning "whether or not those mechanisms correspond to the 'correct' account".
requirements: Verbal responses must be transcribed and coded by trained coders; the article required two independent coders agreeing on 87% of codes before discussion
constraints: The framework assesses the substance of reasoning about causal mechanisms, not its correctness relative to the canonical account
target_learners: College students in introductory algebra-based physics
target_learning_goals: Constructing causal mechanistic explanations of physical phenomena
examples: A chaining example: a student linked the entity moisture and its property of being a conductor to explain why rubbing hands together produces no sparks
key_sources: Conlin, L. D., Gupta, A., Scherr, R. E., & Hammer, D. (2006). The Dynamics of Students' Behaviors and Reasoning during Collaborative Physics Tutorial Sessions. Physics Education Research Conference proceedings record. https://www.compadre.org/PER/
